title: Switch 2 security takes a hit as hackers unlock homebrew access
gist: Researcher Sammy Hajhamid (Pepsipu) used OpenAI's Codex to find a 32-bit integer overflow in the Switch version of SmileBasic 4, then chained it with a FileSystem services buffer overflow. The result is a tethered, software-only userland jailbreak of the Switch 2 that runs homebrew and mods on firmware 23.0.1. Nintendo has already delisted SmileBasic 4 and will likely patch the flaw. The hack is far less serious than the unpatchable 2018 Switch exploit, but it is a bad sign for Switch 2 software security just over a year after launch.

insights.claim: Security researcher Sammy Hajhamid used OpenAI's Codex with a custom harness to probe the language interpreter in the Switch version of SmileBasic 4. The harness sent USB commands to the console, read results via HDMI and power-cycled it with a Bluetooth switch-flipping device. After about two weeks it found a 32-bit integer overflow in array item removal.
insights.speaker: Sammy Hajhamid
insights.so_what: AI coding agents are cutting the effort needed to find console and embedded-system exploits, which raises security costs for platform holders.

insights.claim: The SmileBasic integer overflow on the Switch 2 exposes an array pointer that gives read-and-write access to parts of system memory. Hajhamid then found a buffer overflow in the console's FileSystem services module that exposed a cached data pointer, which gave arbitrary read-and-write privileges and led to native code execution through a faked filesystem process.
insights.speaker: Sammy Hajhamid
insights.so_what: Chained bugs in system modules point to systemic weaknesses in Nintendo's software sandboxing.

themes.theme: Scope and limits of the Switch 2 hack

insights.claim: The Switch 2 userland exploit lets users run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod games, back up save files and access most peripherals through MMIO. Hajhamid demonstrated it with modded characters in Mario Kart World.
insights.speaker: Sammy Hajhamid
insights.so_what: Homebrew and modding communities are moving quickly on the Switch 2, and broader piracy tooling could follow.

insights.claim: The current Switch 2 exploit only gives userland access, which keeps homebrew in a relatively small sandbox and falls well short of the kernel-level access needed for full hardware control.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Full piracy-capable control is not here yet, so the near-term revenue risk to Nintendo is limited.

themes.theme: Nintendo's response and the security cycle

insights.claim: Nintendo has delisted SmileBasic 4 from the Switch eShop worldwide, just as it pulled the 3DS version after the 2016 smilehax exploit. A Japanese demo that may work similarly is still available, and other hackers are teasing similar exploits through other games.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Delisting the entry point slows the exploit's spread but does not stop it if other games turn out to be vulnerable.

insights.claim: The exploit works on the latest Switch 2 firmware (23.0.1), but Kyle Orland expects it to be patched in upcoming firmware releases. Those updates will be required for continued access to many Nintendo services and future games.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Because updates are required for online services, Nintendo can contain software-only exploits.

insights.claim: The Switch 2 exploit is far less damaging than the "unpatchable" original Switch exploit from 2018, which forced Nintendo into a full hardware redesign. Kyle Orland still argues that getting this far just over a year after launch is a bad sign for how secure Nintendo's system software is.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Hardware recall-level risk is avoided, but expect an ongoing cat-and-mouse fight between hackers and Nintendo.
